rows.verified: Employers should assess the known and associated health and safety risks arising from shift work.
HSE's shift-work management approach follows the principles assess, act, check and review.
Shift schedules should plan an appropriate and varied workload.
Employers should offer a choice of permanent or rotating shifts and try to avoid permanent night shifts.
Shift rotation should generally occur every 2 to 3 days or every 3 to 4 weeks; otherwise forward rotation should be used.
Shifts should generally be limited to 12 hours including overtime, or 8 hours for night, demanding, monotonous, dangerous or safety-critical work.
Workers should be encouraged to take regular breaks, and schedules should consider vulnerable workers.
Consecutive working days should normally be limited to 5 to 7, with long, night and early shifts restricted to 2 to 3 consecutive shifts.
Fatigue controls depend on shift pattern, workload, overtime, commuting, worker vulnerability, supervision, alertness and safety-critical consequences.
Shift-work evidence is organisation-, schedule- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level incident probability.
Employers must ensure adequate ventilation in enclosed workplace areas.
Ventilation brings fresh air indoors and removes stale, hot, humid or polluted air.
Natural ventilation uses openings such as doors, windows, trickle vents, air bricks and grilles.
Mechanical ventilation uses fans and ducts to move clean air into and stale air out of rooms.
Risk assessments should identify areas with no effective natural or mechanical ventilation, including break rooms and changing areas.
Stuffy conditions, bad smells and carbon-dioxide monitoring can help identify poorly ventilated spaces.
Natural ventilation can be improved by opening windows, vents and doors, but fire doors must not be propped open.
Recirculated air should be filtered and mixed with fresh air; persistent poor ventilation may require occupancy restrictions or a suitable mechanical system.
Ventilation controls depend on room volume, occupancy, building layout, process heat, pollutants, openings, mechanical-system performance and weather.
Ventilation evidence is building-, room- and operating-condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level indoor-air-risk probability.
